articles.title: Advances in plant polysaccharide research for neurodegenerative diseases therapy.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs), including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease (HD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and multiple sclerosis (MS), represent a growing global public health burden with limited therapeutic options. Plant polysaccharides are natural, biocompatible, and multi-target bioactive macromolecules that have emerged as promising candidates for ND intervention. This review systematically summarizes recent progress in elucidating the structural characteristics, structure-activity relationships, and neuroprotective mechanisms of plant polysaccharides. Key structural features such as molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, glycosidic bond configuration, and spatial conformation critically modulate the biological activity of these molecules. Furthermore, we summarize the numerous protective effects of plant polysaccharides against NDs, including inhibiting abnormal protein aggregation, alleviating oxidative stress via the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway, suppressing neuroinflammation through the NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways, regulating neuronal apoptosis, and modulating the gut-brain axis. Clinical translation challenges, primarily blood-brain barrier penetration, structural heterogeneity, and insufficient clinical validation, are discussed. Future directions include developing advanced delivery systems, conducting large-scale randomized controlled trials, and exploring synergistic combination therapies. Collectively, plant polysaccharides show considerable promise as potential multi-target candidates for the intervention of NDs, although further studies are needed to clarify their therapeutic potential and facilitate clinical translation.

articles.title: Clinical and biochemical characterization of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in a CHCHD10 R15L family.
articles.abstract: Familial forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are potential candidates for gene-directed therapies, but many recently identified genes remain poorly characterized. Here, we provide a comprehensive clinical, neuropathological and biochemical description of familial ALS (fALS) caused by the heterozygous p.R15L missense mutation in the gene CHCHD10. Using a cross-sectional study design, we evaluated five affected and nine unaffected individuals from a large seven-generation pedigree with at least 68 affected members. The pedigree suggests a high (68%-81%) but incomplete disease penetrance. Through cloning of the disease allele from distant members of the family, we establish the disease haplotype in the family. Notably, the haplotype was distinct from that of a previously reported p.R15L mutation carrier with ALS, demonstrating that the variant is in a mutational hotspot. The clinical presentation was notable for being highly stereotyped; all affected individuals presented with the rare ALS variant flail arm syndrome (FAS; also known as brachial amyotrophic diplegia or Vulpian-Bernhardt syndrome), suggesting greater involvement of the cervical spinal cord. Consistently, neuropathology from one family member demonstrated substantially increased CHCHD10 protein aggregation and neuronal loss (though absent TDP-43 pathology) in the cervical versus lumbar spinal cord. This FAS phenotype could be captured by a simple timed finger-tapping task, suggesting potential utility for this task as a clinical biomarker. Additionally, through analysis of fibroblast lines from 12 mutation carriers, isogenic induced pluripotent stem cells and a knock-in mouse model, we determined that CHCHD10 with the R15L variant is stably expressed and retains substantial function both in cultured cells and in vivo, in contrast to prior reports. Conversely, we find loss-of-function (LoF) variants are more common in the population but are not associated with a highly penetrant form of ALS in the UK Biobank (31 in controls; 0 in cases). Together, this argues against LoF and in favour of toxic gain-of-function as the mechanism of disease pathogenesis, similar to the myopathy-causing variants in CHCHD10 (p.G58R and p.S59L). Finally, through proteomic analysis of CSF of variant carriers, we identify that CHCHD10 protein levels are elevated approximately 4-fold in mutation carriers, and that affected and unaffected individuals are differentiated by elevation of two neurofilaments: neurofilament light chain (NfL) and peripherin (PRPH). Collectively, our findings help set the stage for gene-directed therapy for a devasting form of fALS, by establishing the likely disease mechanism and identifying clinical and fluid biomarkers for target engagement and treatment response.

articles.title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

articles.title: Current findings, application, and diagnosis of magnetic resonance imaging in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorder within the motor neuron disease (MND) spectrum, characterized by progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons. The clinical phenotype ranges from pure motor syndromes to forms with cognitive and behavioral impairment, and the pathological burden extends beyond the motor system. Diagnosis remains primarily clinical, supported by electrophysiology and exclusion of mimics. Therefore, objective imaging biomarkers are urgently needed. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is widely used as an auxiliary and differential diagnostic tool in ALS. T1- and T2-weighted imaging can assess cortical thickness, gray matter atrophy, and signal changes. Diffusion tensor imaging probes white matter microstructure. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy detects neurochemical alterations. Resting-state functional MRI assesses functional connectivity and network organization. Susceptibility-weighted imaging is sensitive to iron and calcium deposition. Ultra-high-field MRI provides higher resolution and improved metabolite quantification. This critical review summarizes current findings on MRI in ALS, but importantly organizes the evidence by the specific question being addressed: pathological/histological correlates, diagnostic or discriminatory performance, and clinical associations with phenotype, severity, progression, and prognosis. We also discuss major limitations, including methodological heterogeneity, limited standardization, small and clinically heterogeneous cohorts, frequent use of healthy rather than disease controls, and scarce multicenter validation. Although advanced MRI has revealed robust group-level alterations, none of these techniques has yet become established in routine clinical diagnosis of ALS. We, therefore, distinguish promising research findings from validated clinical biomarkers and outline priorities for future translation.

articles.title: HML-2 env knockdown by AAV9-mediated miRNAs attenuates amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-like manifestations in mice.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease, for which there is no cure. Although the precise aetiology of ALS remains elusive, growing evidence suggests a pathogenic role for human endogenous retrovirus-K (HERV-K) in ALS. Expression of HERV-K subtype HML-2 envelope protein in neurons causes neurotoxicity in vitro and induces ALS-like symptoms in mice. We investigated the use of adeno-associated virus-9 (AAV9)-mediated artificial microRNA (amiRNA) targeting the HML-2 env gene in an ALS mouse model. From an in vitro screen of amiRNAs targeting the HML-2 env gene, three were chosen and inserted in tandem into an AAV9 vector and validated in vitro. This approach provided robust silencing of the transgene, with tandem amiRNA achieving robust reduction in gene and protein expression levels. Its therapeutic effectiveness was tested in an HML-2 Env transgenic mouse model, in which the env gene is expressed under the neuron-specific thy1 promoter and develops an ALS-like phenotype. A single intracerebroventricular injection of AAV9 vector encoding the amiRNAs into the mice at postnatal Day 1 effectively reduced HML-2 Env expression in the brain and spinal cord at 84 days post-injection, which was the latest time point studied. Knockdown of HML-2 env decreased the loss of cortical and spinal motor neurons and alleviated muscle fibre degeneration and fibre-type grouping. This led to improved motor function. Our results provide compelling evidence supporting the use of multiple amiRNAs delivered in an AAV9 vector for treating forms of ALS linked to HML-2.

articles.title: Integrative spatial metallomics: a tutorial review of multimodal elemental imaging workflows, challenges and opportunities.
articles.abstract: Spatially resolved molecular assays are increasingly used to study human health and disease, revealing complex tissue organization beyond what is accessible through bulk analyses. While spatial transcriptomic, metabolomic, and proteomic approaches have rapidly matured, quantitative mapping of metals and trace elements in biological tissues and biominerals through elemental imaging remains comparatively nascent. Elemental distributions alone often provide limited biological interpretation without contextualization within the tissue microenvironment. Here, we summarize themes and computational strategies for integrating spatial elemental data with histopathology and complementary spatial molecular assays. We highlight multimodal approaches for tissue alignment, pixel-wise clustering, and correlative analysis, illustrated through limited use cases involving amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and kidney stone formation. In the ALS cohort, pixel-level elemental profiles were clustered and compared with annotated tissue structures. In the kidney stone cohort, spatial gradients and correlations in elemental and biomolecular features from the renal papilla through the medulla to cortex were examined. Finally, we discuss key challenges for cross-sample, cohort-level analyses, including differences in spatial resolution, normalization, tissue architecture, and mechanistic inference. Addressing these challenges will require interdisciplinary collaboration, enhanced biobanking practices, and development of computational and statistical frameworks.
