articles.title: Liposomal Delivery of a Riluzole-Butyric Acid Mutual Prodrug Enhances Neuroprotection and Cognitive Recovery in Experimental Alzheimer's Disease.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline, impaired synaptic signaling, and persistent neuroinflammation. Current therapies primarily provide symptomatic relief and have limited effects on disease progression. Riluzole, approved for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, exhibits neuroprotective effects through modulation of glutamatergic signaling, but its poor oral bioavailability limits its therapeutic potential. Butyric acid, a short-chain fatty acid postbiotic produced by gut microbial fermentation, possesses well-established anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties. In this study, a mutual prodrug of riluzole and butyric acid was synthesized and encapsulated into liposomes to investigate its effects on drug distribution and preclinical efficacy. The prodrug-loaded liposomes exhibited an average particle size of 322 nm, zeta potential of -7.95 mV, and entrapment efficiency of 43.49%. Oral administration significantly improved cognitive performance and attenuated neuroinflammation and oxidative stress in an AlCl 3 -induced AD-like rat model. Administration of prodrug-loaded liposomes led to the highest concentrations of riluzole in brain homogenates among the relevant treatment groups. Overall, the prodrug-loaded liposomes demonstrated better therapeutic efficacy than the prodrug suspension, individual drug-loaded liposomes, and their respective conventional formulations. The enhanced therapeutic performance is attributed to the complementary pharmacological actions of riluzole and butyric acid, combined with the ability of the liposomal system to improve drug bioavailability and facilitate cerebral delivery.

articles.title: Protein Isoaspartate Repair in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: An Integrative Bioinformatic Analysis of the PCMT Gene Family.
articles.abstract: Protein homeostasis is a fundamental determinant of neuronal survival, and its disruption contributes to the pathogenesis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Protein L-isoaspartate O-methyltransferases (PCMTs) are evolutionarily conserved proteins involved in the recognition and processing of damaged proteins through the repair of isoaspartyl residues and protein quality-control pathways; however, their potential involvement in ALS remains largely unexplored. Here, we performed a comprehensive in silico characterization of the PCMT family (PCMT1, PCMTD1, and PCMTD2) by integrating structural, transcriptomic, single-cell, genetic, and protein modeling analyses. Domain analysis demonstrated that all three proteins share a conserved PCMT domain, while predicted S-adenosylmethionine-binding motifs were identified in PCMT1 and PCMTD2 but not PCMTD1, indicating evolutionary conservation with functional divergence. Expression profiling revealed that PCMT family genes are expressed in ALS-relevant tissues and broadly distributed across neuronal, glial, vascular, and immune cell populations in both healthy and ALS-associated brain single-cell data sets. Analysis of multiple independent ALS transcriptomic cohorts identified consistent upregulation of PCMT family members, with PCMTD1 exhibiting the most reproducible disease-associated expression changes across nervous system tissues and peripheral blood. Gene set correlation analyses further revealed distinct relationships between PCMT expression and neuronal pathways, with PCMT1 showing positive associations with axonal transport and synaptic signaling, whereas PCMTD1 and PCMTD2 displayed largely inverse correlation patterns. Rare missense variants identified in ALS patients were predicted to impair protein function and decrease protein stability, while structural modeling suggested that several substitutions may disrupt conserved residues and the local protein architecture. Collectively, these findings identify the PCMT family as previously underexplored candidates associated with ALS and provide a comprehensive framework for future mechanistic studies investigating their roles in neuronal protein homeostasis and neurodegeneration.

articles.title: A validated antibody toolbox for ALS research.
articles.abstract: A substantial fraction of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-associated proteins remains poorly characterized, in part because of the limited availability of validated research antibodies. We established knockout (KO)-based antibody characterization workflows and demonstrated that widely used antibodies against the major ALS-associated protein C9orf72 lacked specificity (Laflamme et al., 2019). We subsequently scaled this framework to systematically benchmark research antibodies, revealing that up to 61% fail to perform as recommended by manufacturers (Ayoubi et al., 2023b). Here, we extend this approach by establishing the ALS-Reproducible Antibody Platform (ALS-RAP), a comprehensive effort to generate a publicly available dataset of KO-validated antibodies targeting proteins encoded by ALS risk genes. In total, we characterized 303 antibodies against 33 ALS-associated proteins to identify high-quality reagents for use in western blot, immunoprecipitation, and immunofluorescence. Using these antibodies, we profiled protein levels across human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary neurological cell types. These analyses revealed diverse cellular distributions and higher levels of several ALS-associated proteins in glial populations, consistent with emerging evidence for immune contributions to ALS. Together, ALS-RAP provides a validated antibody toolbox and protein expression resource to support the study of ALS-associated proteins.

articles.title: Cancer versus Non-Cancer Patients Admitted to Hospice: a comparison study.
articles.abstract: Malignant disease remains the leading reason for hospice admission, and direct, patient-level comparisons of cancer and non-cancer patients within the same residential hospice are scarce. To compare sociodemographic and clinical characteristics, symptom burden, nutritional support, length of stay and outcome between oncological and non-oncological patients admitted to a single hospice. Prospective observational cohort study of 175 consecutive admissions over one year, after removal of duplicate records. Patients were classified as oncological (n=151, 86.3%) or non-oncological (n=24, 13.7%) based on structured case report form fields. Sociodemographic, functional (Karnofsky Performance Status, KPS), nutritional, symptom (Edmonton Symptom Assessment System, ESAS) and cognitive (Memorial Delirium Assessment Scale, MDAS) data were collected at admission (T0); ESAS completion was also examined at 1 week (T7). Categorical variables were compared with the chi-square or Fisher's exact test, continuous variables (reported as median and interquartile range, including ESAS and MDAS scores) with the Mann-Whitney U test; p-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (q). Most non-oncological patients had a neurological disease (21/24), mainly neurodegenerative diseases, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and dementia. Non-oncological patients were older (median 78.5 vs 72 years, P=0.002, q=0.012) and had worse performance status at admission (median KPS 20 vs 30, P<0.001, q=0.006). Artificial nutrition was more frequent among non-oncological patients (37.5% vs 14.9%, P=0.018), although not after correction for multiple comparisons (q=0.060). MDAS scores were higher in non-oncological patients (median 13 vs 4, P=0.021). ESAS data were missing in about half of oncological and three quarters of non-oncological patients; no ESAS item differed between groups after correction for multiple comparisons, and the non-oncological group's valid ESAS sample fell to a single patient by T7. Length of stay (11 vs 8 days, P=0.518) and in-hospice mortality (80.0% vs 70.8%, P=0.455) did not differ significantly. In this single-centre series, non-oncological patients, mostly affected by neurological diseases, were admitted older, more functionally compromised and with higher MDAS scores than oncological patients, despite comparable length of stay and mortality. Apparent differences in symptom burden are confounded by substantial, likely informative, missing data and should be interpreted with caution. Whether these differences reflect later referral or the age profile of the underlying diseases cannot be determined from these data.
articles.journal: Journal of pain and symptom management

articles.title: Clinical Variability and Genotype Driven Outcomes in an International Cohort of 14 Pediatric FIG4 Patients.
articles.abstract: Biallelic FIG4 variants classically cause distinct conditions characterized by peripheral neuropathy (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4J) or skeletal dysplasia (Yunis-Varón syndrome). However, central nervous system involvement is increasingly recognized. The prevalence and specific characteristics of movement disorders within FIG4-related disease remain poorly characterized, prompting a need to redefine its clinical continuum. To delineate the phenotypic spectrum of FIG4-related disorders beyond established entities (Yunis-Varón syndrome, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4J, bilateral temporooccipital polymicrogyria, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis type 11) using an international multicentre cohort. We retrospectively analyzed clinical, genetic, and neurophysiological data from patients with biallelic FIG4 variants to redefine genotype-phenotype correlations, focusing on motor development, cognitive status, and movement disorders. Evaluating 14 pediatric FIG4 patients revealed a continuous phenotypic spectrum rather than the clinical entities previously described in the literature. Instead of the typical peripheral neuropathy classically associated with pathogenic FIG4 variants, the predominant clinical picture in this age group was a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. Patients showed profound motor and cognitive delay, with a subset additionally displaying distinct movement abnormalities such as dystonia and bradykinesia. Loss of functional FIG4 causes a broader and more severe disease spectrum with central nervous system involvement, including intellectual disability and movement abnormalities such as dystonia and bradykinesia. Recognizing these features should prompt clinicians to consider FIG4-associated disorders, allowing for optimized patient care and tailored therapeutic strategies.
articles.journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology

articles.title: Personalizing nutritional care in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS): a multi-perspective qualitative focus group study of experiences and challenges.
articles.abstract: Background : Proactive, timely nutritional care is important for people living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (plwALS), as weight loss and malnutrition are associated with faster disease progression and shorter survival. However, previous studies have shown that there is considerable practice variation in nutritional care, and that care is not always delivered proactively. Objectives : To gain insight into how healthcare professionals (HCPs), plwALS and their primary caregiver experience nutritional care. Methods : A generic qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured focus group discussions. Five focus group discussions were organized: two with HCPs and three with plwALS and their primary caregivers. Data were transcribed verbatim and analyzed inductively using thematic analysis. Results : In total, 14 HCPs, 19 plwALS, and three primary caregivers participated. Analyses resulted in four major themes: (1) A gap between knowing and acting, (2) balancing providing and withholding care, (3) sufficiently informed to participate in shared decision-making? and (4) opportunities for improvement. Conclusion : Findings suggest that improving nutritional care in ALS requires clear and transparent communication to ensure that plwALS and caregivers are well-informed about the importance of nutrition and monitoring of nutritional status, and more involved in clinical decision-making. Clear explanations about the dietitian's role and nutritional care process may improve patient engagement and facilitate shared decision-making.

articles.title: Subtype and stage inference of tract-level diffusion abnormalities in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) shows substantial heterogeneity in clinical presentation and white matter involvement, but conventional diffusion tensor imaging analyses provide limited information on whether tract-level abnormalities follow distinct patient level patterns. This retrospective secondary analysis included 73 patients with ALS and 30 healthy controls. Fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) from 11 predefined tracts were used as SuStaIn biomarkers, with healthy controls providing the normative reference for Z-score standardization. SuStaIn subtypes and stages were examined against Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R), King's stage, and peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD). The three-subtype model classified patients into cingulate callosal motor mixed subtype (n = 34), hippocampal cingulum posterior projection subtype (n = 32), and posterior callosal projection, MD predominant subtype (n = 7). Exploratory comparisons showed lower PSMD in subtype 0 than subtypes 1 and 2 (both p = 0.026), lower ALSFRS-R in subtype 2 than subtype 1 (p = 0.026), and higher SuStaIn stage in subtype 2 than subtype 0 (p = 0.025). Higher SuStaIn stage correlated with higher King's stage (rho = 0.318, p = 0.006) and lower ALSFRS-R (rho = - 0.289, p = 0.013). After adjustment, higher SuStaIn stage remained associated with lower ALSFRS-R (β = - 0.333, p = 0.013) and more advanced King's stage (odds ratio = 1.181, p < 0.001). Tract-level diffusion SuStaIn identified anatomically interpretable patterns of white matter involvement in ALS and provided patient-level stage estimates associated with clinical disease burden.

articles.title: Urinary Dysfunction in ALS Patients: Assessment With the Overactive Bladder Awareness Tool.
articles.abstract: To compare urinary symptom bother and overactive bladder screening positivity between patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and controls using the Overactive Bladder Awareness Tool (OAB-V8). This retrospective study included 101 patients with definite ALS and 324 controls. OAB-V8 scores were compared using Welch's t-test and multiple linear regression adjusted for age and sex with HC3 robust standard errors. Screening positivity (OAB-V8 ≥ 8) was evaluated using Firth's logistic regression adjusted for age and sex. Mean OAB-V8 scores were 14.0 ± 6.8 in ALS patients and 12.40 ± 5.10 in controls (unadjusted p = 0.026). The adjusted mean difference was 1.65 points (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.20-3.10; p = 0.026). Screening positivity was observed in 101/101 ALS patients (100%) and 272/324 controls (84.0%). The adjusted odds ratio was 41.03 (95% penalized profile-likelihood CI 5.75-5205.66; p < 0.001), indicating substantial uncertainty in its magnitude. ALS patients reported modestly greater urinary symptom burden than controls after adjustment for age and sex. These findings support clinical attention to urinary symptoms in ALS but do not establish their underlying urodynamic mechanism.

articles.title: Evidence of White Matter R 2 * Homogenization After Formalin Fixation.
articles.abstract: Disentangling intrinsic susceptibility-driven R 2 * characteristics in white matter (WM) from fixation-related effects using in vivo, postmortem (PM) in situ, and formalin-fixed PM ex situ MRI. DTI and multi-echo gradient-echo MRI were acquired in vivo, PM in situ and PM ex situ. PM cases included neurologically healthy individuals and patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Voxel-wise R 2 * values were obtained using a mono-exponential fit and evaluated both as whole WM averages and according to WM fiber-to-field orientation. For the PM ex situ orientation-dependency analysis, PM ex situ R 2 * data were registered to the corresponding in situ DTI acquisition. Averaged as well as orientation-dependent R 2 * profiles were pooled across WM and compared across conditions. Whole WM averaged and orientation-dependent R 2 * values differed across in vivo, PM in situ, and PM ex situ conditions. No differences were observed between PM in situ healthy and PM in situ ALS cases. Compared with in vivo measurements, both PM conditions showed elevated whole WM averaged R 2 * values and reduced orientation dependency, with the strongest R 2 * anisotropy in vivo and nearly absent orientation dependency in the PM ex situ condition. While orientation-dependent R 2 * is reduced but preserved in unfixed PM in situ tissue, it is largely eliminated after prolonged formalin fixation without rehydration, likely due to microstructural reorganization and protein cross-linking. Collectively, these findings indicate that orientation-dependent R 2 * measured in fixed tissue has limited translational validity, while underscoring its sensitivity to intact microstructural organization in vivo and in unfixed PM tissue.

articles.title: Anatomically Defined Motor Phenotypes Reveal Dissociated Trajectories of Progression, Neurofilament Profiles, and Survival in ALS.
articles.abstract: Clinical heterogeneity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) may reflect structured disease trajectories. This study investigated whether anatomically defined motor phenotypes capture reproducible patterns associated with progression, serum neurofilament light chain (NfL), and survival. In a multicenter cohort of 1307 ALS patients, motor phenotypes were classified by region of onset, timing of propagation to a vertically distant body region (early ≤ 12 months vs. later), and the degree of upper (UMN) and lower motor neuron (LMN) dysfunction. Intercenter consistency was assessed using the Friedman test and Kendall's W. Associations with ALS progression rate (ALSPR), NfL, and survival were analyzed using group comparisons and Cox regression models. Phenotype classification was consistent across centers (Kendall's W 0.75-0.89). Onset phenotypes were significantly associated with ALSPR, NfL, and survival (p < 0.001). Trunk onset showed the lowest log(NfL/ALSPR), indicating dissociation between rapid progression and relative NfL elevation. Early propagation was the strongest marker of disease aggressiveness, with higher ALSPR, elevated NfL, and reduced survival (HR 2.93, p < 0.001). In early propagation, NfL disproportionally increased with progression indicating a relative uncoupling of NfL from functional decline. Phenotypes with balanced UMN/LMN and predominant LMN involvement were associated with shorter survival (HR 2.51, p < 0.001). Anatomically defined motor phenotypes identify reproducible ALS trajectories with distinct clinical and neurofilament profiles. Early propagation provides an actionable risk marker of disease aggressiveness, while combined upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction or lower motor neuron predominance is prognostically unfavorable. These findings support integrating structured phenotyping into prognostic models and clinical trial stratification.

articles.title: Copper-Mediated Radiofluorination of the Excitatory Amino Acid Transporter 2 (EAAT2)-Targeted PET Tracer [ 18 F]RP-115: Alternate Synthetic Method.
articles.abstract: Excitatory amino acid transporter 2 (EAAT2) is a key regulator of extracellular glutamate in the central nervous system. Dysregulated EAAT2 is implicated in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), highlighting EAAT2 as a potential target for PET imaging. We previously reported a multistep radiosynthesis of [ 18 F]RP-115, a CNS-permeable prodrug that undergoes esterase-mediated hydrolysis in the CNS to yield the active EAAT2-binding carboxylate. Motivated by recent advances in copper-mediated radiofluorination (CMRF), we sought to develop a more efficient late-stage radiosynthesis of [ 18 F]RP-115. A two-step radiosynthesis of [ 18 F]RP-115 using CMRF provided [ 18 F]RP-115 in high radiochemical yield (52.8% ± 2.1 %, decay-corrected from starting [ 18 F]fluoride ion, n = 4), high molar activity (355 ± 61 GBq/μmol), and high radiochemical purity (> 99%) with a total synthesis time of 70 min. Chiral HPLC analysis demonstrated that the configuration of the aspartic acid residue remained intact without racemization during both the CMRF and trifluoroacetic acid mediated deprotection. We developed an efficient radiosynthesis of [ 18 F]RP-115 via CMRF, achieving high radiochemical yield and molar activity. This efficient synthesis may serve as a basis for the future implementation of a CMRF-based automated radiosynthesis of [ 18 F]RP-115.

articles.title: Mitochondria-Associated Membranes as a Convergent Hub of Brain Aging: From Neurodegeneration to Cerebral Ischemia.
articles.abstract: Brain aging is the principal risk factor for both neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) and cerebral ischemic disorders, yet the subcellular mechanisms linking these conditions remain incompletely defined. Mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs)-specialized contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria-sit at the intersection of two well-established hallmarks of aging, mitochondrial dysfunction, and loss of proteostasis, making them an attractive mechanistic node for understanding age-related brain decline. In this review, we propose a MAM-centered framework that unifies neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathology under the broader paradigm of brain aging. We first summarize the molecular architecture of MAMs and their core functions in neuronal Ca 2+ transfer, mitochondrial dynamics, lipid metabolism, inflammasome assembly, and autophagic quality control, together with emerging evidence from non-neuronal brain cells. We then examine how MAM dysfunction intersects with five hallmarks of aging-mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of proteostasis, disabled macroautophagy, chronic inflammation (inflammaging), and altered intercellular communication-drawing on evidence from physiological aging and cellular senescence models. Next, we discuss disease-specific roles of MAMs in cerebral ischemia and in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington's disease. A central theme emerges: Rather than a unidirectional decline of MAMs, brain aging is associated with a loss of MAM homeostasis, in which both insufficient and excessive ER-mitochondria coupling can be pathological and the shared deficit is the failure to maintain contact-site function within an optimal range. Finally, we consider age-relevant therapeutic and biomarker strategies targeting MAMs and their potential translation into geriatric neurology. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate MAM biology across physiological brain aging, cerebral ischemia, and the four major NDDs within a single homeostatic framework, offering a unified perspective on the mechanisms of age-related brain decline.

articles.title: Neural stem cell-derived small extracellular vesicles ameliorate disease progression in the SOD1 G93A murine model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that primarily affects motor neurons leading to muscle weakness, paralysis, and ultimately, respiratory failure. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) facilitate intercellular communication by mimicking the functions of their parent cells. In this study, we found that repeated administration of neural stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (NSC-derived EVs) improved motor performance and provided protection to lumbar motor neurons, the neuromuscular junctions, and muscle morphology in the SOD1 G93A transgenic mouse model of ALS. Furthermore, by analyzing the RNA-sequencing of muscle specimens from ALS-SOD1 patients, we demonstrated that the rescue effects of NSC-derived EVs might be linked to the p53 pathway. Compared to the PBS control treatment group, both TP53 and the p53 upregulated modulator of apoptosis (PUMA) were downregulated in the spinal cord of mice treated with NSC-derived EVs. These data provide additional knowledge for the promising use of NSC-derived EVs as a potential therapy for ALS.
articles.journal: Journal of neuropathology and experimental neurology

articles.title: Neuroepigenetics of the Environmental Exposome: Molecular and Clinical Implications in Neurodegeneration.
articles.abstract: Neuroepigenetics studies the molecular mechanisms that regulate gene expression in the nervous system without altering the DNA sequence. The environmental exposome has emerged as a key factor influencing neuronal plasticity and brain homeostasis, contributing to vulnerability to neurodegeneration. This narrative review analyzes the role of neuroepigenetic reprogramming as a central mechanism linking chronic environmental exposures with neurodegenerative diseases. Evidence indicates that alterations in DNA methylation, histone remodeling, and microRNA regulation contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and chronic neuroinflammation. These mechanisms are critically involved in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Neuroepigenetics represents a central mechanistic axis in neurodegeneration by integrating environmental exposures with intrinsic biological processes. This framework offers new opportunities for the development of early biomarkers and targeted preventive and therapeutic strategies.

articles.title: Patient and public involvement in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis research in Japan: a survey through nationally advertised ALS Café events and a pilot advocacy training program.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) remains an incurable, progressive neurodegenerative disease. Patient and public involvement (PPI) has been increasingly recognized as a means to enhance the relevance, quality, and efficiency of research; however, its implementation in intractable neurological disease research remains limited in Japan. This webinar-based study, conducted through nationally advertised ALS Café events, aimed to clarify current PPI awareness among the Japanese ALS community and to explore strategies for promoting patient advocacy. Data were collected during the "ALS Café" held in September 2024 and a subsequent patient advocacy training program organized in October 2025. Among 79 respondents (42 patients with ALS and 37 caregivers), approximately 80% reported being unfamiliar with the concept of PPI, yet 72.2% expressed willingness to participate once the concept was explained. Among the 57 respondents willing to participate, interest was highest for involvement in translating research findings into practice (56.1%) and in identifying research themes (47.4%), and most (93%) stated that they expected no remuneration beyond reimbursement of expenses. The subsequent training program was well received, with mean evaluation scores exceeding 8.0 on a 0-10 scale, indicating high comprehensibility among participants (changes in knowledge or willingness to participate were not assessed). Respondents were a self-selected group of ALS Café participants with limited demographic characterization who may not represent patients and caregivers who do not participate in such events, and the training program evaluation lacked a pre-training baseline; these limitations should be considered when interpreting our findings. These findings reveal substantial stated willingness among Japanese patients with ALS and their caregivers to contribute to research despite low baseline awareness of PPI. This gap between limited awareness and high stated willingness suggests that targeted educational efforts could meaningfully expand patient engagement in ALS research. Systematic awareness-building initiatives, structured and accessible engagement opportunities, and sustained collaborative relationships between researchers and the patient community are essential for strengthening patient advocacy and accelerating drug development for ALS in Japan. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a serious disease that damages the nerves controlling movement, and there is currently no cure. Researchers are increasingly encouraged to work together with patients and members of the public — an approach known as patient and public involvement, or PPI — to make research more relevant and useful. However, little was known about how familiar Japanese patients with ALS and their families are with PPI, or whether they would want to take part in it.We asked people with ALS and their caregivers who attended an online event called the “ALS Café” in September 2024 to complete a questionnaire about PPI. Of the 79 people who responded, about 80% had never heard of PPI before. Even so, once we explained what PPI means, more than 70% said they would like to be involved in research. Most people wanted to help make sure that research findings are put into practice, and wanted to help choose which questions researchers should study. Most people did not expect to be paid for their time, although many wanted their expenses covered.Based on what we learned, we then created a training program to help patients and caregivers understand ALS research and how they could become involved. We delivered this training in October 2025, and it was very well received, with high understanding scores across all 14 topics covered.Our findings show that although PPI is not yet well known among Japanese patients with ALS, there is strong interest in taking part once it is explained clearly. We believe that ongoing education, together with accessible and low-burden ways to get involved, could help more patients and families take part in ALS research in Japan, which may in turn help speed up the development of new treatments.

articles.title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
articles.abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

articles.title: Ataxin-2 loss flips a metabolic switch for neuron health.
articles.abstract: Gastaldo et al. 1 report that lowering ataxin-2 protects neurons from TDP-43 toxicity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis by activating neuronal glycolysis and astrocytic cholesterol synthesis, not by reversing TDP-43-dependent molecular pathology. The downstream effectors, IDH1 and HMGCS1, thus emerge as candidate therapeutic targets.

articles.title: Beyond the Larynx: New Insights Into Upper Airway Responses to Mechanical Insufflation-Exsufflation.
articles.abstract: This case report describes a 44-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and ineffective secretion clearance despite home use of mechanical insufflation-exsufflation (MI-E). He reported upper airway obstruction, respiratory discomfort and recurrent aerophagia during therapy. Dynamic assessments using transnasal flexible laryngoscopy and videofluoroscopy under different MI-E settings showed that upper airway responses were strongly influenced by inspiratory flow, pressure levels, expiratory time and cervical positioning. Higher inspiratory flow and pressure induced supraglottic closure and airflow diversion to the oesophagus. In contrast, lower inspiratory flow combined with reduced expiratory pressure and shorter expiratory time improved glottic opening, maintained airway patency and enhanced cough mechanics. Spontaneously adopted cervical extension optimized airflow and minimized oesophageal insufflation, whereas neutral alignment impaired cough efficiency. These findings emphasize the importance of individualized MI-E settings and patient-specific biomechanics in optimizing therapy in ALS.

articles.title: Characterization of plasma misfolded superoxide dismutase 1 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: To characterize the dynamics of plasma misfolded superoxide dismutase 1 (mSOD1) and evaluate its utility as a state-dependent biomarker for patient stratification and therapeutic monitoring in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). We utilized an SOD1/G93A mouse model and a cohort of 160 ALS patients, including four with SOD1 mutations, 12 with non-SOD1 mutations (C9orf72, TARDBP, FUS, OPTN), and 144 with nongenetic ALS. Chemical precipitation and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay were used to quantify mSOD1 levels in plasma, spinal cord extracts, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Clinical outcomes were assessed by the annual reduction in the revised ALS Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R) score and ventilator-free survival. In mice, plasma mSOD1 increased at the late symptomatic stage with subsequent numerical decline at the humane endpoint, accompanied by progressive motor neuron loss and increasing mSOD1-associated pathology. In humans, mSOD1 was elevated in 100% of SOD1-mutant, 25% of non-SOD1-mutant, and 22.2% of nongenetic ALS patients. Elevation was state-dependent, enriched in patients with moderate disability (ALSFRS-R 17-45). Plasma and CSF mSOD1 levels were correlated across the overall ALS cohort, but this association was no longer significant after exclusion of SOD1-mutant ALS cases. In one tofersen-treated patient, plasma mSOD1 showed rapid, parallel, and sustained reduction with CSF levels. No significant differences in clinical outcomes were observed in nongenetic ALS based on mSOD1 status. Approximately 22% of nongenetic ALS patients exhibit elevated plasma mSOD1, primarily during the moderate disease stage. Plasma mSOD1 is a candidate state-dependent biomarker for biological stratification and may have potential for treatment monitoring.

articles.title: Feasibility of Longitudinal Home Monitoring of Nocturnal Transcutaneous CO 2 and Relationship to Standard Respiratory Measures in Patients With ALS: A Pilot Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) results in respiratory muscle weakness causing hypoventilation, retention of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), and chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure. In this pilot study, we performed a 12-month assessment of daytime and home nocturnal CO 2 to track respiratory progression, determine relationships with surrogate respiratory measures, and assess the impact of non-invasive ventilatory support. Adults with forced vital capacity (FVC) less than 90% predicted secondary to ALS were recruited from two sites in the northeast US. Participants were followed up at standard visits every 3 months for up to five visits. Spirometry, functional scores, and patient-reported outcomes of dyspnea were recorded. Each visit included a 15-min, seated measurement of transcutaneous CO 2 (PtcCO 2 ) while in clinic, followed by 3 nights of home overnight PtcCO 2 monitoring. Linear mixed-effects models were employed to describe the changes that occurred longitudinally and resulting from the initiation of non-invasive ventilation (NIV). Sixteen subjects were enrolled, with nine completing the full study. Strength and FVC declined over time, while daytime PtcCO 2 remained stable. Five individuals demonstrated nocturnal hypercapnia that preceded FVC < 50% predicted normal. Transition to NIV was associated with a 7 mmHg decrease in nocturnal PtcCO 2 . Home nocturnal PtcCO 2 assessment in ALS may identify respiratory insufficiency prior to FVC. Transcutaneous CO 2 may play a role in the respiratory management of patients as a biomarker for hypoventilation risk and NIV titration. However, equipment availability and data quality limitations would benefit from professional assistance rather than independent in-home use.

articles.title: Lack of NRF2 expression alters the dynamics of stress granules promoting the aggregation of ALS disease-associated proteins.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor neuron death. Although ALS pathogenesis is multifactorial, increasing evidence highlights a close interplay between dysfunction of RNA metabolism and redox imbalance in disease progression. Redox perturbation converges with RNA dysregulation at the level of the dynamics of stress granules, transient ribonucleoprotein assemblies implicated in protein aggregation, in ALS. The redox-sensitive transcription factor NRF2 (Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2) plays a pivotal role in cellular homeostasis, yet its function and regulation remain poorly defined in ALS. In this study, we explore how NRF2 modulates stress granule dynamics under oxidative and non-oxidative stress conditions. Using live-cell imaging, we reveal that NRF2 deficiency enhances the formation of stress granules in response to oxidative and non-oxidative stressors, facilitates their persistence, and promotes increased stress granule recruitment of ALS-linked proteins such as TDP-43 and FUS. Likewise, we uncover a protective role of pharmacological NRF2 activation in limiting exacerbated stress granule responses in iPSC-derived motor neurons from C9orf72-ALS patients and show how NRF2 activation can impact TDP-43 aggregation and loss of function in SH-SY5Y cells. Together, these findings position NRF2 as a crucial integrator of redox signalling and RNA metabolism in ALS pathogenesis. Targeting NRF2 may offer novel therapeutic avenues to counteract the vicious cycle of oxidative stress, dysfunctional stress granule dynamics, and protein aggregation in motor neuron disease.

articles.title: The impact of diagnostic criteria on the detection of nocturnal hypoventilation in adult amyotrophic lateral sclerosis patients.
articles.abstract: Nocturnal hypoventilation (NH) is an early manifestation of respiratory muscle weakness in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and plays a key role in determining the optimal timing for non-invasive ventilation (NIV). However, several diagnostic definitions of NH have been proposed, and their impact on NH prevalence remains unclear. In this cross-sectional study, 56 non-ventilated ALS patients underwent home-based overnight monitoring with transcutaneous carbon dioxide (TcCO 2 ) and pulse oximetry. NH prevalence was assessed using seven definitions derived from daytime arterial blood gases, nocturnal oximetry, and TcCO 2 parameters. Agreement between definitions was evaluated using Cohen's and Light's kappa coefficients. NH prevalence varied widely depending on the definition used, ranging from approximately 5% with daytime arterial criteria to 36.7% using peak TcCO 2 ≥49 mmHg. Overall concordance among definitions was low (Light's κ = 0.27), indicating that current NH definitions are not interchangeable. Currently used definitions of NH in ALS show substantial heterogeneity and identify different patient subsets. These findings highlight the need for ALS-specific consensus definitions of NH.

articles.title: The TBK1-OTUB2-IRF3 signalling complex promotes neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.
articles.abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway-mediated chronic inflammation drives neurodegeneration in natural aging and various neurodegenerative diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Here, we identify Otubain-2 (OTUB2) as a pivotal regulator that orchestrates the STING signalosome to amplify inflammatory responses. The function of OTUB2 in neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration was investigated through genetic deletion and pharmacological inhibition of OTUB2 in hTARDBP transgenic mice​, adeno-associated virus-mediated TDP43 overexpression mice, and aged mice. Biochemical assays were performed to dissect underlying molecular mechanisms. OTUB2 inhibited K63 ubiquitination of TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), thereby suppressing TBK1 kinase activity and promoting cell death mediated by hyperactivated receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1). Additionally, OTUB2 functioned as a scaffold facilitating assembly of the TBK1-interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) signalling complex, a prerequisite for IRF3 phosphorylation, and enhanced IRF3 dimerization by reducing its K11 ubiquitination. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of OTUB2 significantly ameliorated neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration in both ALS and aged mouse models. This study establishes OTUB2 as a critical regulator of cGAS-STING signalling and a potential therapeutic target for neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.

articles.title: Combined melatonin and edaravone therapy attenuates methylmercury-induced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-like neurodegeneration through GLP-1 modulation and myelin preservation.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive and fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the selective degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, resulting in progressive muscle weakness, paralysis, and respiratory failure. Despite the availability of disease-modifying therapies, current treatment options provide only modest clinical benefits, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies targeting multiple pathological mechanisms. Melatonin, a pleiotropic neuroprotective molecule with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic properties, has emerged as a promising candidate; however, its influence on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-associated neuroprotective signaling and related molecular events in ALS remains poorly understood. Therefore, the present study investigated the neuroprotective efficacy of melatonin in a methylmercury (MTMR)-induced rat model of ALS and explored its effects on GLP-1-associated molecular alterations, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, neurotransmitter homeostasis, demyelination, and neuronal injury. Molecular docking analysis was performed to predict the interaction of melatonin with proteins implicated in ALS pathology. Adult Wistar rats were exposed to MTMR (5 mg/kg, p.o.) for 21 days to induce ALS-like neurodegeneration, followed by treatment with melatonin (5 or 10 mg/kg, i.p.), edaravone (3 mg/kg, i.p.), or their combination for an additional 21 days. Neurobehavioral performance, biochemical alterations, hematological parameters, molecular biomarkers, and histopathological changes were subsequently evaluated. MTMR administration produced profound motor deficits accompanied by reduced GLP-1 levels, neurotransmitter imbalance, increased neuroinflammatory and apoptotic markers, elevated neurofilament light chain (NEFL), skeletal muscle injury, methylmercury accumulation, and extensive myelin and neuronal damage. Melatonin treatment significantly attenuated these pathological alterations in a dose-dependent manner by increasing GLP-1 levels, improving antioxidant status, reducing inflammatory and apoptotic responses, restoring neurotransmitter balance, preserving myelin integrity, and improving neuronal morphology across multiple brain regions and the spinal cord. Molecular docking further predicted favorable interactions between melatonin and several proteins associated with ALS pathophysiology, supporting its potential as a multitarget therapeutic agent. In most outcome measures, combined treatment with melatonin and edaravone produced greater neuroprotective effects than either intervention alone. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that melatonin substantially attenuates methylmercury-induced ALS-like neuropathology through coordinated modulation of multiple pathological processes associated with neurodegeneration. Although the precise molecular mechanisms require further experimental validation, the observed restoration of GLP-1 levels together with improvements in oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, apoptosis, neurotransmitter homeostasis, and myelin integrity suggests that melatonin may represent a promising adjunctive therapeutic strategy for ALS.

articles.title: Immunometabolic dysregulation of reactive microglia and astrocytes in neurodegenerative diseases: Mechanistic insights and therapeutic implications.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) are increasingly understood as multifactorial disorders characterized by intertwined pathological processes, in which metabolic dysfunction may act as a critical and potentially disease-amplifying contributor to the proteinopathy-driven pathological cascade. Despite growing recognition that microglial and astrocytic metabolism governs central nervous system tissue damage-repair homeostasis, intercellular metabolic crosstalk between glia and neurons remains insufficiently synthesized across major NDDs. This review delineates how core metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, mitochondrial respiration, lipid processing, and amino acid transport, shape glial reactivity in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. We highlight glial metabolic reprogramming, a proposed theoretical framework arising from severe glial metabolic dysregulation. Within this framework, persistent pathological stress may drive reactive glia to sequester local energy substrates in excess, which is hypothesized to trigger bioenergetic failure in neighboring neurons. Broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory agents show poor clinical performance because they only block cytokine outputs rather than reverse glial metabolic exhaustion. Therapeutic efforts should therefore shift toward restoring glial metabolic flexibility. Cell-type-specific metabolic reprogramming, instead of pan-metabolic suppression, may circumvent systemic adverse effects. Precision strategies targeting such intercellular metabolic imbalance could provide promising cell-resolved metabolic avenues to retard NDD progression.

articles.title: Improving dysarthric speech classification with generative AI-based data augmentation.
articles.abstract: Dysarthria is a neurological speech disorder characterized by impaired motor control of speech production, resulting in reduced intelligibility. It commonly arises in the context of neurodegenerative conditions, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and cerebral palsy. The development of deep learning systems for dysarthria assessment is hindered by the scarcity of annotated data, which restricts the ability of models to generalize to unseen speakers. This study proposes a cross-corpus diffusion-based data augmentation strategy for improving automatic speech intelligibility classification from dysarthric speech. A Grad-TTS model is trained on dysarthric speakers from the TORGO dataset and used to synthesize the vocabulary of UA-Speech, producing speaker-conditioned samples intended to transfer pathological acoustic traits across corpora. The proposed strategy is evaluated both independently and in combination with conventional signal-level augmentation using ResNet-50 and ResNet-152 classifiers in binary and four-class intelligibility classification tasks. The results indicate that cross-corpus synthetic augmentation improves average performance and that, in most settings, its integration with conventional augmentation yields further gains, suggesting that the two strategies introduce complementary forms of variability.

articles.title: Longitudinal coagulation-fibrinolysis dynamics are associated with survival in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Background : Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) has been associated with thromboembolic risk. However, whether dynamic coagulation-fibrinolysis markers provide prognostic information in ALS remains insufficiently defined. Methods : We conducted a prospective cohort study of 151 patients with ALS, including repeated coagulation measurements in a longitudinal subset ( n = 58), and assessed directional validation in the independent Answer ALS (AALS) cohort ( n = 270). Survival analyses, longitudinal modeling, and plasma proteomic analyses were used to examine associations between coagulation-fibrinolysis dynamics, functional decline, and survival. Results : Higher baseline fibrinogen (FIB) was independently associated with shorter survival (HR = 2.19; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.40-3.44). In the longitudinal subset, a steeper increase in D-dimer (DD) was associated with shorter survival (HR = 1.012; 95% CI, 1.001-1.024) and lower ALSFRS-R scores over time ( β = -0.013; 95% CI, -0.016 to -0.009). Directionally consistent validation was observed in AALS using rescaled SomaScan-derived DD trajectories (HR = 1.0002; 95% CI, 1.0000-1.0004). Plasma proteomics showed reduced tetranectin, a fibrinolysis-related protein, in ALS; slower tetranectin decline was associated with longer survival using rescaled SomaScan-derived tetranectin trajectories (HR = 0.996; 95% CI, 0.993-0.998). Conclusions : These findings suggest that longitudinal coagulation-fibrinolysis markers may help identify a survival-related biomarker profile in ALS, involving higher baseline FIB, steeper rising DD, and reduced or more rapidly declining tetranectin.

articles.title: Microglial perturbation in heavy metal-induced neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration: mechanisms, phenotypic plasticity, and therapeutic prospects.
articles.abstract: Heavy metal exposure has emerged as a significant environmental contributor to neurodegenerative disease, and a substantial body of mechanistic evidence implicates microglia in the pathological cascades that follow. Lead, cadmium, arsenic, manganese, copper, cobalt, mercury, and zinc disrupt central nervous system homeostasis through multiple cellular targets, but the resident innate immune cells of the brain are well placed to translate these insults into sustained neuroinflammation. Evidence for this critical narrative review was assembled through a purposive search of PubMed, MEDLINE, and Google Scholar for mechanistically informative studies reporting glial endpoints, with reference lists searched by hand and no systematic protocol applied. This review synthesizes current understanding of how individual metals engage microglial signaling networks, with particular attention to oxidative stress, NF-κB activation, NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, MAPK cascades, and suppression of the Nrf2 antioxidant axis. We examine the phenotypic spectrum that extends well beyond the classical M1/M2 dichotomy, including disease-associated microglia, lipid-droplet-accumulating microglia, and interferon-responsive states, and consider how metal-specific signatures map onto these transcriptional programs. Manganese-driven inflammasome assembly, cadmium-induced mitochondrial impairment, lead-mediated disruption of calcium homeostasis, and mercury-evoked autophagic dysfunction are discussed as illustrative examples of mechanistic divergence within a common neuroinflammatory framework. Glial responses to metal mixtures, which better represent real exposure than single-element designs, are considered separately, and the evidence for greater-than-additive effects is appraised. Downstream consequences for astrocyte reactivity, blood-brain barrier integrity, synaptic remodeling, and neuronal viability are placed in the context of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Therapeutic avenues are appraised, including chelation, natural antioxidants, NLRP3 inhibitors, TREM2 modulation, and microglial replacement strategies. Methodological constraints, particularly the overreliance on BV-2 cells and acute high-dose exposure paradigms, are critically considered. The review concludes by identifying priorities for translational research, including longitudinal human cohort studies, single-cell transcriptomic profiling of metal-exposed microglia, and the development of region-specific exposure models that better reflect chronic environmental realities.
articles.journal: Biometals : an international journal on the role of metal ions in biology, biochemistry, and medicine

articles.title: Riluzole-Derived Benzo[d]thiazoles as CK1δ Inhibitors for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis-Related Neurodegeneration.
articles.abstract: Riluzole-derived benzo[d]thiazoles were investigated as metabolite-inspired CK1δ inhibitors, a kinase involved in TDP-43 phosphorylation and therefore relevant to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Starting from the known CK1δ activity of riluzole, we examined whether its major hydroxylamine metabolite could preserve target recognition and provide a rational entry point for scaffold optimisation. The metabolite retained CK1δ inhibition, but its limited chemical stability and toxicity in neuronal cells identified the hydroxylamine group as a critical liability. Replacement of this functionality with a hydrazine converted the fragile metabolite-derived structure into a more potent and tractable CK1δ inhibitor series. Structure-activity relationship studies revealed that the hydrazine moiety accommodates broader substitution than the hydroxylamine counterparts, with branched alkyl and benzyl groups giving the most balanced profiles. Docking and molecular dynamics suggested that the improvement could be attributed to an additional hydrogen-bond with Gly86 in the hinge region. The best derivative combined submicromolar CK1δ inhibition with passive blood-brain barrier permeability, short-term cellular tolerance, ATP competitive inhibition, direct target engagement, and preliminary selectivity over GSK3β. Although this compound did not result neuroprotective in an oxidative stress model, it paves the way for a focused benzo[d]thiazole platform for probing CK1δ biology in ALS.

articles.title: Strain-specific morphology and CNS propagation of template-directed SOD1 aggregation following peripheral nerve inoculation.
articles.abstract: Accumulation of misfolded SOD1 protein into intracellular aggregates, in the spinal cord (SpC) and brainstem, is a hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis caused by mutations in the SOD1 gene (SOD1-ALS). Two distinct aggregate conformations, denoted strain A and strain B, were identified in the CNS of SOD1 G85R and SOD1 D90A transgenic (Tg) ALS mouse models, respectively. Both strains transmit templated SOD1 aggregation and ALS-like disease in Tg mouse models when inoculated into the SpC, whereas muscle or intraperitoneal inoculations, of up to 300 times more inoculate, did not. Here, we used strain A and strain B aggregate seeds, prepared from SpCs of the Tg mice, to investigate strain-specific differences in transmission of templated aggregation and ALS phenotype via a peripheral nerve. We show that both strains can transmit templated aggregation to the CNS via the sciatic nerve in SOD1 G85R Tg mice. Strain A resulted in shorter time to disease onset and earlier end-stage disease compared to strain B, and these strain-specific differences were accentuated in the sciatic nerve inoculation model compared to direct SpC inoculations. To further analyse the differences between strain A and strain B, we developed an immunohistochemical method that distinguishes the two SOD1 aggregate strains in tissue sections. This method revealed that strain B adopts an elongated, skein-like morphology, whereas strain A aggregates appear as accumulations of rounded, bead-like structures. These findings suggest that SOD1 aggregates forming in a peripheral nerve might transmit disease to the CNS and that different SOD1 aggregate strains can influence disease onset and progression. Our results warrant further exploratory studies of SOD1 aggregate conformations and their potential role in the manifestation of SOD1 mutant-specific disease phenotypes.

articles.title: The Epidemiological Transition of Neurodegenerative Diseases in China: A Multi-Layered Deconstruction Using Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), including Alzheimer's disease and other dementias (ADOD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and motor neuron disease (MND), represent a mounting public health challenge in China amid rapid population aging. A systematic deconstruction of their epidemiological transition using the most recent data remains lacking. Data from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 were utilized to examine temporal trends (1990-2023) for ADOD, PD, and MND in China. Age-standardized rates of incidence (ASIR), prevalence (ASPR), mortality (ASMR), and disability-adjusted life-years (ASDR) were analyzed. Joinpoint regression was used to identify significant inflection points. Decomposition analysis quantified the contributions of population aging, population growth, and epidemiological change. And bayesian age-period-cohort models projected trends to 2035. From 1990 to 2023, the ASIR for ADOD (EAPC 0.41; 95% CI 0.33 to 0.49) and PD (EAPC 0.84; 95% CI 0.76 to 0.92) rose significantly. Between 2019 and 2023, multiple indicators across the three diseases demonstrated a consistently synchronous upward trend. This acceleration coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic. Decomposition demonstrated that population aging was the dominant driver. Sex-specific disparities were pronounced. Females bore a higher ADOD burden, whereas males predominated in PD. ASIR and ASPR are expected to rise, while ASMR and ASDR are projected to decline for ADOD and PD. For MND, only the ASPR indicated a brief, peaked rise in the predicted trends. In the field of neurodegenerative diseases, China is projected to undergo an epidemiological transition characterized by chronicization. This trend calls for systematic adjustments in healthcare services, long-term care systems, and social support structures. Sex and gender differences further underscore the need for gender-sensitive prevention, clinical management, and care strategies to prevent the further widening of inequalities. Population aging remains a critical factor that cannot be overlooked. Therefore, there is an urgent need to establish a proactive, gender-sensitive framework for system-wide restructuring that incorporates long-term monitoring and oversight.

articles.title: Global best practice recommendations for genetic counselling and testing in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with substantial clinical and genetic heterogeneity. Advances in ALS genomics, emerging gene-targeted therapies, and genotype-specific clinical trials have increased the importance of genetic counselling and testing for individuals with ALS and their families. However, access to these services remains highly variable globally due to disparities in healthcare infrastructure, laboratory capacity, specialist availability, and funding. Existing guidance has largely been developed in high-resource settings and may not be feasible or equitable worldwide. The International Alliance of ALS/MND Associations convened an international, multidisciplinary Genetics Task Force to develop expert consensus recommendations for genetic counselling, genetic testing, and laboratory practice in ALS across diverse geographic and resource settings. Recommendations were developed through a structured, iterative consensus process incorporating clinical expertise, lived experience perspectives, published evidence, and global representation. Final recommendations were reviewed and approved through anonymous voting at an in-person consensus meeting. The resulting recommendations establish both minimum and aspirational best practices, emphasizing equitable access, informed decision-making, culturally responsive counselling, tiered genetic testing approaches, and context-appropriate laboratory standards. These globally informed recommendations provide a pragmatic framework to support clinicians, laboratories, policymakers, and advocacy organizations in improving access to high-quality ALS genetics services worldwide.
authors: Alliance Genetics Task Force Working Group Members

articles.title: Intracisternal injection of two human SOD1 aggregate strains induces templated aggregation and ALS in transgenic mouse model.
articles.abstract: Cytosolic aggregates containing misfolded superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1) protein is an established hallmark of ALS caused by mutations in the SOD1 gene. We have previously identified two structurally distinct strains of human (h) SOD1 aggregates (denoted A and B) in mice transgenic (Tg) for hSOD1. Strain A and B have both been shown to transmit templated aggregation and induce early-onset of fatal ALS-like disease when injected directly into the spinal cord or peripheral nerve of hSOD1 Tg mice. In contrast, peripheral administration of hSOD1 aggregates into the intraperitoneal cavity or skeletal muscle did not induce disease. Collectively, these studies provide insight on the spreading mechanism of SOD1. However, the complete map of propagation routes and underlying mechanisms utilized by SOD1 aggregates in ALS is not fully charted. Here, we investigated whether hSOD1 aggregates may spread to the central nervous system (CNS) via the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Mutant hSOD1 aggregate seeds or control samples prepared from spinal cords of hSOD1 Tg mice or non-Tg mice, respectively, were inoculated into the cisterna magna of adult 100-day-old Tg mice expressing the G85R mutated hSOD1 protein. Disease phenotyping as well as biochemical and immunohistochemical analyses were performed and compared across the experimental groups. The mice inoculated with hSOD1 seeds developed early signs of ALS by 90 days after inoculation and reached terminal stage approximately 180 days earlier than mice receiving control seeds. Additionally, both strain A and B were observed to initiate templated aggregation along the neuroaxis. The results show that hSOD1 aggregates are capable of transmitting from the CSF to the CNS where they induce ALS-like pathology and concomitant phenotype. Unraveling the propagation pathways utilized by SOD1 opens new avenues to assess treatment strategies against ALS.

articles.title: Neuromuscular junction pathology in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and emerging molecular therapeutic strategies.
articles.abstract: Traditionally conceptualized as a soma-centric pathology, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal, heterogeneous neurodegenerative disease. The suboptimal outcomes of central nervous system (CNS)-directed therapeutic strategies have necessitated a shift in focus toward the dying-back hypothesis. This hypothesis contends that synaptic disconnection and axonal retraction at the distal neuromuscular junction (NMJ) are early pathological events that may antedate overt motor neuron loss. This review systematically examines the NMJ as an early vulnerable and therapeutically tractable peripheral niche in ALS pathogenesis, rather than merely a downstream consequence of proximal proteinopathy. Evidence from human clinical samples and ALS mouse models, particularly SOD1-G93A mice, collectively supports the early vulnerability of the NMJ, with the temporal precedence of denervation, synaptic retraction, and mitochondrial dysfunction most clearly demonstrated in experimental models. We highlight how the breakdown of the tripartite synapse-comprising the motor terminal, skeletal muscle, and terminal Schwann cells (tSCs)-may disrupt essential neurotrophic signaling and local metabolic homeostasis. Furthermore, we discuss how advancements in humanized in vitro NMJ models and spatial transcriptomics provide unprecedented resolution into localized RNA dysmetabolism and bioenergetic failure. Finally, we evaluate emerging therapeutic strategies specifically designed to stabilize or restore the NMJ, including MuSK agonists and other NMJ-directed approaches. By recontextualizing the NMJ as a critical early site of vulnerability, we propose that targeting the peripheral synaptic microenvironment may offer a promising strategy for modifying the progression of ALS.

articles.title: Persistent and compartmentalized T cell immunity in ALS.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal neurodegenerative disease increasingly linked to T cell responses, although the mechanisms driving T cell activation and disease progression remain unclear. Here we used single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing, longitudinal immune profiling and imaging flow cytometry to identify long-lived intrathecal clonotypes and antigen-presenting cell-T cell complexes displaying features of immunological synapse formation, consistent with intrathecal antigen presentation. Higher frequencies of CD4 + effector, CD4 + regulatory and CD8 + T cells in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were associated with slower disease progression, whereas increased circulating CD4 + effector and regulatory T cells were associated with faster progression. T cell clonotypes shared between blood and CSF exhibited distinct transcriptional states. Finally, frequencies of cytomegalovirus-specific T cells in CSF and anticytomegalovirus serum antibodies were correlated with faster progression and shorter survival in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. These findings reveal compartmentalized immune dynamics, largely contrasting protective intrathecal responses with harmful systemic activation.

articles.title: Rate and Shape of Functional Decline in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Identify Clinically Distinct Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Phenotypes.
articles.abstract: The ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised decline rate compresses trajectory shape into a single number, potentially missing distinct phenotypes. We tested whether shape identifies phenotypes that rate does not distinguish, and whether post-hoc analysis recovers a hidden ultrarapid subgroup. From the Piemonte and Valle d'Aosta register (2000-2022), we applied 2 models to 1,686 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis patients: a Gaussian mixture model (GMM; rate axis) and a latent-class mixed model (LCMM) with cubic splines (shape axis). Concordance, prognostic performance, calibration, and clinical utility were assessed at 24 months. External validation used the Emilia-Romagna register. The rate model identified 4 classes (GMM-Slow 31%, GMM-Inter-slow 46%, GMM-Inter-fast 17%, GMM-Catastrophic 6%; slopes -0.44 to -3.52 points/month); the shape model 4 (LCMM-SlowLinear 46%, LCMM-PlateauFall 23%, LCMM-LateDecline 15%, LCMM-RapidEarly 16%). Concordance was modest (kappa = 0.273). Adding shape to rate changed discrimination negligibly (C-index 0.761 vs 0.755), but separated subgroups within rate classes (within GMM-Catastrophic, 30.1 vs 12.0 months). LCMM-LateDecline combined moderate early decline with reduced respiratory reserve (median forced vital capacity 83.5%) and 22.7-month median survival. The combined model gave the greatest net benefit for the composite outcome. Of 945 patients excluded for sparse sampling, 367 were ultrarapid progressors with shorter survival than LCMM-RapidEarly; findings replicated in the Emilia-Romagna register. Rate and shape describe partially overlapping aspects of the disease. LCMM-LateDecline, with moderate early decline yet occult respiratory compromise, is clinically challenging, and the 3-visit criterion hides over half of ultrarapid patients. Rate predicts the overall burden of progression, whereas shape predicts the timing of deterioration. ANN NEUROL 2026.

articles.title: Structural Social Connection, Biological Ageing, and Neurodegenerative Disease Burden: A Global Ecological Analysis of Household Size and Modelled Dementia Incidence Estimates.
articles.abstract: Poor social connection and ageing-related biological processes are recognised contributors to Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. However, cross-national evidence linking structural indicators of social connection with dementia and broader neurological dis-ease burden remains limited. This ecological study examined country-level associations be-tween average household size and modelled neurological disease incidence estimates. Country- and territory-level data from up to 204 settings were analysed. Average household size was the primary exposure, and model-derived, age-standardised incidence-rate estimates for Alzheimer's disease and other dementias were the primary outcome. Par-kinson's disease, motor neuron disease, multiple sclerosis, idiopathic epilepsy, headache dis-orders, and total neurological disorders were examined as comparative secondary outcomes. The Henneberg Index, life expectancy at age 60, GDP per capita, and urban living were in-cluded as contextual covariates. Analyses included Pearson and Spearman correlations, par-tial correlations, principal component analysis, and multivariable linear regression. Household size was strongly and inversely associated with Alzheimer's disease and other dementias incidence estimates (Pearson r=-.841, p<.001). The association remained after adjustment for the included covariates (β=-.569, p<.001). Significant inverse adjusted associations were also observed for Parkinson's disease, motor neuron disease, and total neurological disorders, whereas patterns differed for other neurological outcomes. Principal component analysis identified a single ageing-development dimension explaining 72.1% of the variance, with household size loading inversely against life expectancy at age 60, econom-ic affluence, urban living, and the Henneberg Index. Smaller average household size was associated with higher modelled incidence estimates for dementia and selected neurodegenerative diseases at the country level. These findings should be interpreted as ecological associations rather than evidence of individual-level causation and suggest that household structure is embedded within broader demograph-ic, socioeconomic, and ageing-related processes.

articles.title: TDP-43 dysfunction destabilizes glial homeostatic identity in ALS/FTD.
articles.abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) pathology is a defining feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Although TDP-43 dysfunction has traditionally been studied through a neuron-centric framework, increasing evidence demonstrates that astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes are also directly affected and actively contribute to disease progression. In this review, we examine how TDP-43 dysfunction disrupts lineage-specific glial homeostatic programs and promotes distinct pathological state transitions across major glial populations. In astrocytes, TDP-43 dysfunction impairs neurotransmitter regulation, metabolic and neuronal support, RNA homeostasis, and secretory signaling while promoting inflammatory and antiviral-like states. In microglia, altered TDP-43 disrupts inflammatory regulation, phagocytosis, lysosomal function, lipid metabolism, and stage-dependent protective responses. In oligodendrocytes, TDP-43 dysfunction compromises RNA processing, lineage maintenance, lipid metabolism, myelin integrity, and long-term axonal support. Together, these findings suggest that glial TDP-43 dysfunction cannot be reduced to a single generalized form of reactivity but instead reflects the breakdown of distinct cell type-specific identities required to maintain central nervous system homeostasis. A cross-glial framework integrating cell-autonomous dysfunction, non-cell-autonomous signaling, disease stage, and genetic context may therefore provide a more complete understanding of TDP-43 proteinopathy and its contribution to neurodegeneration across the ALS-FTD spectrum.

articles.title: The "Invisible Killer" of Neurodegeneration: Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurodegenerative Disorders, Mechanisms, Emerging Pathways and Therapeutic Strategies.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease (PD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), Huntington's disease (HD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) place substantial burden on global public health. Mounting evidence identifies mitochondrial dysfunction as a central contributor to neuronal damage and progressive brain functional decline. As a narrative review, this work aims to dissect mitochondrial‑associated pathological features across these major neurodegenerative disorders, summarize under‑recognized emerging mechanisms, and highlight translational bottlenecks for mitochondrial‑targeted therapies. Mitochondria sustain neuronal survival by mediating oxidative‑phosphorylation‑driven energy production, biomolecule biosynthesis, calcium homeostasis, reactive oxygen species (ROS) metabolism, and apoptotic regulation. In PD, aggregated α‑synuclein (α‑syn) damages respiratory‑chain complex I, perturbs mitochondrial dynamics and blocks PINK1/Parkin‑dependent mitophagy. In AD, amyloid‑β together with hyper‑phosphorylated tau (p-Tau) impairs respiratory complex activity, axonal mitochondrial trafficking and mitophagic clearance. Mutant huntingtin induces multiple mitochondrial lesions in HD, while inflammation‑triggered oxidative stress secondarily compromises mitochondrial function in MS. Pathogenic mutations in ALS disrupt respiratory‑chain assembly, mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy. Beyond classic mitochondrial defects including respiratory‑chain impairment, dynamic imbalance and defective mitophagy, emerging mechanisms such as mitocytosis, mitochondrial aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase (mt‑aaRS) dysfunction and mitochondria‑associated membrane (MAM) disruption are discussed. Mitochondrial dysfunction drives neurodegeneration via energy exhaustion, aggravated oxidative stress, pathological protein aggregation and excessive neuronal apoptosis. We further recapitulate mitochondrial‑oriented therapeutic approaches including small‑molecule regulators, mitophagy activators, mitochondrial biogenesis promoters, gene‑editing strategies and mitochondrial transplantation. Notable translational obstacles remain, including limited blood‑brain‑barrier penetration of candidate drugs, narrow therapeutic time‑window post‑symptom onset, and prominent disease heterogeneity. By synthesizing basic experimental findings and pre‑clinical and clinical trial progress, this review provides updated insights into the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases and facilitates the development of precise mitochondrial‑targeted therapeutic regimens.

articles.title: Time-to-Event Analysis of Clinical Milestones in the ALS Natural History Consortium Dataset.
articles.abstract: Study of clinical milestones, particularly intermediate events like loss of ambulation, in large amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cohorts is limited. Here, we leverage the ALS Natural History Consortium dataset to evaluate the time-to-event for several outcomes and prognostic factors that predict risk. Longitudinal data from 1950 participants were used in time-to-event analyses based on time from diagnosis. Outcomes were gastrostomy, loss of ambulation, loss of useful speech, non-invasive ventilation (NIV) usage, and death equivalent (death or mechanical ventilation). Median times-to-event were calculated along with Kaplan-Meier curves. Cox proportional hazards models for each outcome estimated (through adjusted hazard ratios [HR]) the impact of several prognostic factors, including sex, region of onset, age at diagnosis, and the initial rate of change (delta-FRS) in ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) scores. Estimated median times-to-event for clinical outcomes ranged from 1.44 to 6.21 years, with a median time to death equivalent of 2.12 years. A higher delta-FRS was the greatest risk factor for all outcomes (HRs between 2.01 and 3.05). Limb onset decreased risk of loss of speech, NIV use, gastrostomy, and death equivalent (HRs 0.41-0.78). Older age at diagnosis increased risk of gastrostomy, NIV use, and death equivalent (HRs 1.08-1.27). These findings further inform expectations of time to various outcomes, especially rarely investigated intermediate events, and their risk factors. The importance of progression rate supports other recent findings, highlighting delta-FRS as a key prognostic factor with potential utility in clinical trial designs.
